comments.author: ion_trapper
comments.content: The valuation of a company is what the last purchaser of its stock agreed to pay for it. There is no simple accounting formula that takes revenue and outputs that number. It is strictly a measure of what the last buyer thought the company was worth. That buyer may have used revenue in their calculations of worth, or maybe not. Maybe it was expectation of future revenue growth. Maybe they just liked the name.This sounds arbitrary until you appreciate that the ones with most purchasing power on the market are also the same ones who have previously proven themselves to be capable asset allocators, as proven by their ability to accumulate capital. So the valuation of a company is not just every random Joe’s opinion equally averaged, but weighted towards those whose opinions on value have previously tended toward being correct (this includes capital acquired by any means, not just equity trading. For example, if you earned a lot of money with your own product, you have proven yourself to be able to judge value and effectively allocate resources too).The market starts to make a lot more sense when you start to use it as an oracle of hidden information (“what is the market telling me about the value of X?”) instead of an irrational adversary (“why is the price Y? That doesn’t make sense!”).

Maybe it was expectation of future revenue growth. Maybe they just liked the name.This sounds arbitrary until you appreciate that the ones with most purchasing power on the market are also the same ones who have previously proven themselves to be capable asset allocators, as proven by their ability to accumulate capital. So the valuation of a company is not just every random Joe’s opinion equally averaged, but weighted towards those whose opinions on value have previously tended toward being correct (this includes capital acquired by any means, not just equity trading. For example, if you earned a lot of money with your own product, you have proven yourself to be able to judge value and effectively allocate resources too).The market starts to make a lot more sense when you start to use it as an oracle of hidden information (“what is the market telling me about the value of X?”) instead of an irrational adversary (“why is the price Y? That doesn’t make sense!”).

comments.content: I think a lot of it boils down to "constitutional AI".They did a paper on this a long time ago[1], I'm sure they have altered their techniques some, but I this was the earlier signal that they really treated the AI as a separate entity and trained it as such. And focus not just on it's capability, but it's *behavior*, when to push back on the user, etc... Imo. it's more about the philosophy of the constitution in this paper than the specific RLAIHF, I'm sure this idea of "when to follow instructions and when to trust yourself is in their system prompts for all their RL environments, and even their rewards.This idea of an objective function vs what the model should do during human interaction is a huge question and a very subtle one to get right, but it's why they were winning in real world application even before they were winning in raw benchmarks.Especially in the era of RL environments dominating more and more compute it's vey easy to overfit a model to be very good at accomplishing a narrow task exactly as specified. Much more complicated to have it respond appropriately on turn 5 of a nuanced conversation with a user about their private codebase.[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073

comments.author: lionkor
comments.content: The rewrite it in rust crowd is getting a major thing wrong; rewriting without sufficient (lived) knowledge of the original will usually end in disaster.This is why people (including me), who absolutely adore Rust, make fun of the RiiR crowd. If you think a rewrite from the ground up is the best way to approach making software safer, you've lost the plot entirely.Let's say you rewrite your terminal emulator in Rust from C or C++; you'll first undo decades of bug fixes, compatibility decisions, quirks, etc. which you WILL have to deal with eventually. This essentially puts you back at least a decade, because these issues take users using the software to point out to you before they're fixed. The only benefit of this whole game being that you get memory safety. These teams are never the original teams, which is the source of the problem. A rewrite can only succeed if it's a result of all the learned failures and shortcomings of the original, otherwise it's bound to repeat every single mistake and add more on top.And you don't even deliver memory safety to the users of the original this way, because people won't use the rewrite, because it's buggy, incompatible, etc.

comments.author: jillesvangurp
comments.content: We tried it out for a few weeks earlier this year with a small team. It's alright but there are some annoying defaults (no link previews by default being one of the more annoying ones). You have to opt in to that on every channel for every user. I get why they did that but basically usability and UX is thrown under the bus here because of some hypothetical privacy issues.That's nice if you are genuinely paranoid on this front (rightfully or otherwise) but really sucks if you want people to share links with each other (one of the big use cases we seem to have for using tools like this).Related to that, a side effect of all the e2e encryption is that it's really hard to give people or agents access to the full history of a channel. It's not impossible but it involves jumping through some hoops. And of course a primary reason for us switching away from Slack was using AI agents in our chats more and experimenting with running some of our own bots and something that is sometimes referred to as a company brain.Instead of fighting the tool we switched the tool. We picked Zulip around the same time the founders of that project were hired by Anthropic. For the migration, I gave AI access to my matrix keys and it moved over most of our channels to Zulip. Since Zulip has topics, I also made it group messages by topic.I like Zulip so far. They could use a UX refresh in the client. It looks a bit dated and meh. But otherwise it does the job. With both Zulip and Matrix, I orchestrated the rollout and hosting with AI, including giving admin privileges to manage the whole thing. Works surprisingly well with both. But jobs like add this person to that channel and given them such and such rights are working flawlessly. We had some openclaw thing running for a while but we gave up on that (too much issues with that). But we have a lot of chatgpt scheduled automations and some scripts and skills that allow it to search through and post in Zulip channels. Very useful.If you don't want to self host, Zulip has a generous freemium tier as well in their managed hosting. Haven't tried it but looks like a decent starting point if you want to try it out. You can migrate to self hosted later, if you want.

comments.author: george_max
comments.content: We've had spectacular infrastructure outages for decades; I think that a cluster of incidents in one week doesn't establish that AI is directly responsible for declining reliability.IMO, the issue is that AI is reducing the cost of building and modifying systems much faster than it's reducing the cost of understanding them. For example, an engineer can work on a problem or project for a week that could otherwise be done by AI in an hour or so. But, that week spent was not "wasted time"; it was understanding what it is they are building, discovering undocumented assumptions, knowing about different dependencies, developing intuitions about the system and how it works, etc.This causes comprehension debt. Yes, the system does ultimately work, the tests  also pass. But the level of comprehension goes down significantly.That said, AI can also help reduce this debt by asking it what you need help understanding.A good blog post on this: https://larsfaye.com/articles/ai-coding-will-prevent-experti...

comments.author: black3r
comments.content: "Smart" is a word we label for someone who possesses enough "intelligence", "knowledge" or "experience". These are 3 separate capabilities, which work together well and can to a certain point complement each other.Generative AI started with lots of "knowledge", and has since been trained on lots of practical examples to give it lots of "experience". AI has significantly more "knowledge" and "experience" than a human can attain during his lifetime. But it isn't and can't be "intelligent".It can't "think outside the box", it doesn't have "intuition", it doesn't know how to "ask the right questions"... It can simulate all three if the problem you point it at is related to the "knowledge and experience" it has, or by the sheer fact of letting it run a long time until it figures out the right solution by just analyzing lots of unneeded paths inside its 1M context window.If you're smart and want to see it's "non-intelligence" in action, just turn on the extended thinking summaries and watch it work in real time on some harder task, like debugging some non-trivial bug. It's initial intuition is often very wrong, it often presumes something to be true without asking or checking, or double checks stuff that do not need double checking, if it sees contradictory evidence, it can't properly assess what's going on...The thing is - if you don't see this (and most people won't cause by default it doesn't show you its process, you have to turn it on) - and just let it run for an hour or two, it often eventually does arrive at the correct conclusion - and you may consider it smart for figuring it out, even if you yourself could've figured that out 2x faster, but were too lazy to dig deep.Another very good example of AI's non-intelligence is its tendency to over-engineer solutions, especially on smaller projects. That's again caused by its lack of intelligence. For lots of coding tasks it produces 3-10x the amount of code needed, because it also thinks about "edge cases" that can't happen in the project, it assumes the project has much bigger scale than it does, etc... Lots of people call AI "smart" for this, because "it thought of things I haven't thought of", not realizing they're unnecessary, and thus being the "opposite of smart".That's what's meant by the "illusion of intelligence".

comments.author: dofm
comments.content: > These are 90-95% cheaper than Anthropic. I'd prefer open source, too, but this has nothing to do with Windows Phone OS (which failed because of network effects).FWIW it is worth noting that the GP's suggestion is more in line with Microsoft's own stated belief in the future of "unmetered AI".At the moment, Microsoft is arguably meeting that claim with their support for and encouragement of Nvidia Nemotron Bolt, which is an actually pretty good, quite interesting, unusually-trained-and-sized-to-fit MoE model that was designed to go with the launch of the Nvidia/Microsoft RTX Spark machines.(Good Sam Witteveen video about it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WJpeW9lCSUM )But it would be good to see Microsoft themselves distilling an open weights model.Like any vendor with a profit motive they do have to decide the obvious, though: how do you make money from it, when right now it could cost several hundred million dollars to train (even if you adjust the training of a larger proprietary model so you can distill the smaller one from it)?There is, essentially, no way to keep an open weights model from being copied/distilled/extracted, and IMO what that tends to suggest is that open weights models will essentially gravitate to sort of uncontroversial, "standard library" tasks.So I think it also means that Microsoft's approach on open weights will ultimately be the same as Apple's: they will focus their efforts on LLMs that meaningfully add function to their OS and can be decapitated to make similarly useful decision models.Put another way: given the geopolitical angle of the last few weeks, I think it is possible that the open weights coding models we have now may be among the best we will ever get, until the nearly inevitable GPU/tensor hardware glut arrives.In the meantime, something else is clearly happening: much broader competition in the "good enough" models category, which is what we need to drive down the cost of inference hardware such that open source and open weights are feasible over the longer term.

comments.content: The Chaimberlain / MyQ situation is terrible. I strongly recommend avoiding them all together.I recently installed a Chaimberlain garage door opener in a location that required three buttons inside the garage. comments.author: dj68k
comments.content: Chalk me up to another happy user of Ratgdo. I got one of the older ESP8266-based ones whose Homekit firmware has been in "maintenance mode" by the developer due to its board having limited RAM and processing power to do the things they're doing with the current boards. That was a bummer to find out since I'd had the thing for less than a year and I was using the "dry contact" system: manually wired magnetic switches on the door to tell the board whether the door is up, down, or in a state between (opening or closing). It's a very, very old garage door opener.Since the code was put in a "best-effort basis" for future updates, it's gone from version 2.2 to 2.2.6 with numerous fixes. Most notable was software-configurable "debounce" functionality which finally solved my problem with the door tripping the magnetic reed switches several times quickly when the door comes to a stop and confusing the board about its current up/down status.I bring it up because I have tremendous enthusiasm for people who take an idea, a cheap microcontroller, and put together a solution for people who prefer to stick with older, simple appliances but still want some sort of smart functionality. People who "make cool stuff and put it on the internet." That the creator disclosed that he's putting his focus on the newer boards and will maintain/fix issues with the older ones on a "best-effort" and then actually does it... it's fantastic. Because of this continued support and fixes, I can't recommend Ratgdo boards enough.

comments.author: lucasluitjes
comments.content: From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"):> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.And the "Limitations" section:> There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.

comments.author: ievans
comments.content:
Super impressive work by Calif as usual.The exploit conditions are very specific but there are still going to be a lot of hosts impacted. We at Semgrep published some free detection scripts here: https://github.com/semgrep/detection-scripts/tree/main/CVE-2...They look for these five conditions:  * HotSpot VM: any OpenJDK build, Oracle JDK, or GraalVM JDK. Only HotSpot generates the stub. OpenJ9 and GCJ are OK. Azul Prime (Zing), which replaces C2 with its own JIT, and any VM name not recognized as HotSpot are [?], never [!].
  * x86-64 JVM on an x86-64 host.
  * Version 17.0.6 or later, not at or above a version listed in FIXED_IN, and no newer than the newest releases checked (see below). Newer versions are [?]: they may carry the fix.
  * The JVM reports avx512_vbmi and avx512bw, and UseAVX >= 3.
  * Base64 intrinsics are on and C2/JVMCI can compile. These turn it off: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, -Xint, -XX:TieredStopAtLevel below 4.

comments.author: Pokepokalypse
comments.content: Truth be told; as far as I can tell, the output the human gets from the AI can vary vastly in quality, depending on guardrails on the AI side. Guardrails that are internal (and opaque) to the user, combined with directives the user sets up, often manually.(for example, I have mine keep ready reference to all of our CMMC controls and best practices)- and not only will my sessions cite referenced material as it responds, but it will do so when it writes code, as well - and it does a pretty decent job of keeping me honest. The one bit I'm struggling with is limiting complexity when it designs a solution to a problem. For larger projects, this can snowball quickly - and I haven't found an effective way to prevent this yet.Skills can be shared, but it's a bit of a steep climb to getting an entire organization to pick the same skill (to get consistent behavior across the whole org)- sometimes an individual skill as it's written, will conflict with some other personal standard or quirk of how they work, so it's difficult to share them.   This really seems, to me, to be very similar to how the software world used to work (as far as interoperability goes), earlier in history when there weren't many open standards, (and NO open source code) -  and every competing OS vendor was trying to destroy their competitors so they could become a monopoly.But yes, there's quite a bit of effort now that goes into maintaining this personal harness, and I'm sure the even smarter folks will come along and figure out workable ways of standardizing and sharing those kinds of harnesses.I've been in this industry for 30 years, and the way I work has always changed with the times and new tools.  It changed a LOT when Dev Ops became a thing. IaC, and containers.  This feels kind of like that change, but maybe an order of  magnitude. Almost feels like going from assembler to learning something like python; in terms of how much abstraction is being added.

posts.title_cn: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
posts.abstract: 讨论要点：Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. ...

comments.author: natch
comments.content: Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).

comments.author: imeanwhatdoikno
comments.content: If you look at valuation of a company like Micron (MU), it's pretty clear that the market expects a collapse in their profits. They are growing at absolutely insane rates, whether you look at YoY (well over +300%) or QoQ (over +40%) in both revenue and profits. Yet their PE is below 10. SK Hynix is similar.A typical company that trades at a sub-10 PE is a flatline-to-dying business whose last juice is being squeezed out before the inevitable sale of remaining valuable assets and dissolution.Of course the current market price is not a perfect predictor of the future of a business but despite all the memes and anecdotes, the market is far more often basically right than dramatically wrong (it's just that when it does get things dramatically wrong, that's what gets all the publicity, for obvious reasons).So, assuming the market is roughly right in its valuation of Micron or SK Hynix, either demand will collapse or supply will surge or, some combo of the two. Either way it seems extremely likely that within a couple of years at most the prices of DRAM and NAND will come waaaay down.

posts.title_cn: Do not buy RAM, compress
posts.abstract: 讨论要点：As others have said, macOS does this by default and it's quite impressive. I have a long running daemon with a memory leak. By its nature, the leaking memory is very repetitive and easily compressed. ...

comments.author: varenc
comments.content: As others have said, macOS does this by default and it's quite impressive. I have a long running daemon with a memory leak. By its nature, the leaking memory is very repetitive and easily compressed. Right now this daemon has tried to claim 2.5GB of memory, but it's been compressed to a mere 450MB of actual memory! And because it's a memory leak, it never accesses this old stuff, so it never gets decompressed. Only 20MB of RAM is held that isn't compressed.Of course, it would be far better to just not have the memory leak...but in the mean time, macOS memory compression is making the leak nearly a none issue.

Modern cpu should include more hardware support for memory compression

comments.author: ltrg
comments.content:
I was involved with this project as a reporter, though others from my organisation did most of the work.HN readers may be interested to know a bit about the tech stack. The 15 million or so documents, mostly Outlook mailbox exports, were provided to partners in the consortium via a tool called OpenAleph [1], which is maintained by DARC and based on ElasticSearch and a schema called FollowTheMoney [2], developed specifically for the investigative journalism use case. A lot of the original work on this was done by Friedrich Lindenberg (@pudo), who now runs OpenSanctions [3].The timing was v. interesting given where we are with LLMs -- it's the first major leak I've worked on where it was possible to leverage local models to do some of the heavy lifting, and this only got more possible as the project went on. The coordinators provided a centrally hosted chatbot with RAG, but I also managed to get some surprisingly useful material using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my 24GB M2 MBA via a custom agent harness for Aleph/OpenAleph. [4]Happy to answer any questions about techy stuff, though I'm not a spokesperson for the project by any means. Seen a few people saying "just release the data!", but I think that slightly misunderstands what this work is. The whole point of forming a consortium of hundreds of journalists and sifting through the dump is to identify the bits that are in the public interest to report on -- especially important in jurisdictions like the UK, where I'm based, which have very strong defamation laws. Think Panama Papers, not Wikileaks.[1] https://darc.li/openaleph/
[2] https://followthemoney.tech/
[3] https://www.opensanctions.org/
[4] https://github.com/data-desk-eco/sift

comments.content: I really strongly disagree with this. Let's say you have all the data. You release it. How many people are going to go audit it? Not many. So instead of you, a journalist who actually has a professional interest in this and a reputation to build, you're handing analysis off to clout chasers. Suddenly whoever can find the most explosive viral take will win. Not the most accurate take. The most viral. And the most viral is often something just wrong enough to engage those who want to believe it whilst also engaging those who know enough to refute it - that's where you hit the sweet spot of engagement. Sure someone could go back to the original published data and debunk it - well done, you're driving engagement and uninformed people aren't going to see you debunking it, they're going to 90% see the original false claim, and 10% see a debate they know nothing about which is 50:50 on what they end up believing.Far more effective is for you to listen to different journalists opinions and reporting over time and answer two questions: "Is this person acting with integrity?" and "What are their biases that I need to factor into my analysis". It is much more important to be listening to journalists who have clear ethical standards - even if you disagree with them.

I then used Claude to write a harness in Swift (CLI/menu bar app, see above) that uses one model session to queue a load of tasks for short follow-ups, followed by summarisation, which generated pretty useful Markdown reports on my queries, with links through to Aleph for the originals. comments.author: lrvick
comments.content: For those asking in threads. 4x r9700s will cost about 6-8k depending on how patient you are with ebay auctions.From there any motherboard and CPU that can give you 4x slots of 16x Gen 5 P2P capable PCIe slots positioned such that you can install 4x cards is probably fine. Ideally with a CPU capable of memory encryption.My latest pairing is a ASUS Pro WS W890E-SAGE SE For $800 open box, and a Xeon 654 for $1300. My first build was an AMD EPYC rig for similar cost a few months ago using a Gigabyte ME03-PE0 and a AMD EPYC Siena 8224P for about 2k combined. I specifically wanted one amd and one intel machine for reproducible build diversity which most probably do not care about.Do not get too attached to specific cpus and boards. Get what is available for cheap with the needed pcie bandwidth open box on ebay from reputable sellers to save thousands of dollars.Be sure to get a power supply that can handle all 4 cards. I run Silverstone Hela 2500s at about $800. Do not go cheap on power supplies. It will end in pain. Can confirm.Then 2-3k for 64gb in DDR5 RDIMMs. This is the most painful thing to purchase but it is what it is.Not only do I recommend this setup, I plan to build more of them to share with my team.If you are patient and buy used, a 10k budget can get you a very powerful local AI rig running 100% FOSS software/drivers even today.

comments.author: jkingsman
comments.content: Even dumber local models that are heavily quantized to fit on consumer GPUs can be lovely as a dimwitted household assistant. A lot of people look to offload things they already do to LLMs, which can be great with frontier models, but you've got the highest standards and preferences for tasks you already do, so it's the most likely to fall into a "should have just done that myself" outcome. I've found great success in instead lowering my threshold of things I'd take time to do -- I wouldn't spend time on it, but I'd spend 60s prompting an LLM to take a crack. I'm fortunate to have the hardware to run Qwen 3.8 Flash Next at q8, but most of the tasks I have it do would be totally doable for a mid-quant Qwen 3.8 27b.Some recent tasks I've thrown it:* Go through my blood test data (from EHR XML dumps from prior years) and give me some over-time charts for consistently-sampled measurements* Go through my Good Articles bookmarks, epubify them, and drop one down onto my ereader each morning for my commute, then archive the offline version into cold storage* Go through my music library, identify my most-listened low-bitrate tracks, and source or assemble a shopping cart to get high res versions* Analyze local tax/foreclosure auctions for vacant land; grab aerial screenshots, tax data, ownership data, and compile a weekly report of things maybe worth bidding on based on some specific selection criteria (fun facts: if you're willing to accept some headaches, 5+ acres can be yours for under $5k, if you're in the right area)* Dump my grocery store loyalty data, analyze my purchasing habits, and prepare a weekly instacart for my approval that aims to sync with usage habits. Tweak and learn volume/order adjustments over time.* Given a KVM that can mount ISOs onto the host, reimage two old laptops of unknown status with Debian and install Minecraft so my nieces and I can have a LAN party* Organize my music (high confidence MusicBrainz Picard matches), movies/TV shows, ebooks, and video game ROM collections with metadata and good folder organization* Archive bookmarked fanfiction for my offline library (slowly, and respectfully, and with an actual browser. The browser is anti-bot-countermeasured to the gills, but QFN regularly solves hCaptcha and Cloudflare turnstile challenges. Once I gave it the ability to drag, it even reasonably reliably solves drag-shape captchas. A little while back it made a purchase on eBay which is NOT a bot friendly site.)Would I personally spend time on doing most of these? Generally not. Could an LLM screw them up so badly I regret it? Also generally not. I get the luxury of a psuedo-assistant that doesn't judge how menial the tasks I send it are, and I save time. With a local LLM, my privacy concerns are far less than with frontier models, and local abliterated models are less (or just not at all) twitchy around things that frontier classifiers balk at.I'm hopeful that big projects like Muse can help to normalize menial task offloading, and that local LLMs provide the bridge for more technically minded folks to use them even more aggressively and limitlessly (as in compute limits/subscription costs) and cheaply.

comments.author: herf
comments.content: I love local AI, but even so, I admit the economics point the other way. Unlike gaming, AI is a uniquely good match for data centers because the applications today aren't latency-sensitive at all (except perhaps DLSS/self-driving/robotics). Most importantly, utilization is massively better with always-on servers doing parallelism (in-flight batching). Also in some areas (like California) our local electricity is quite expensive, so moving the work 100ms away can help. The privacy implications are horrifying, though.

comments.author: Tuna-Fish
comments.content: GPU-style platforms (lots of compute connected to a big shared pipe that connects to a large pool of fast memory) are inherently more efficient for centralized inference.Local inference gets truly interesting when the proper next-gen, natively AI and not just a repurposed GPU, stuff starts to land. Initially things like compute-in-memory and fancy flash, and later possibly the truly exotic stuff like various RMM (read-mostly-ram, for example stacked FeFET on logic) tech.IMO there is no chance for ubiquitous local AI to happen if that means people using GPUs. But the industry is chasing all possible solutions for more efficient inference platforms, and if something like pachinko machine architecture with FeFETs ends up winning, suddenly buying a local ai inference solution in a box is no longer as insane.

comments.author: turzmo
comments.content: Physicist here. I don't have time right now to read the papers in depth, nor are the results directly in my area, but I would say a few things.One is that there are a near-infinite number of "open problems" in physics because the surface area of research programs in theoretical physics is extremely large. Before I was in the world of physics, I would have thought that "solving an open problem" meant that physicists around the world would be rejoicing and discussing the result. In reality, other than for the big, field-defining questions, only a small handful of people might care about any problem being solved. That holds true even for the Millennium problems.Even if I were to read these papers in depth and understand them, without talking to somebody that knows the area and what has been done in it already, I would have no sense of the significance. The way to assess significance is to see how the community responds. Only time will tell whether people care about these results enough to cite them, incorporate them in future work, etc.And so, like many other people I know, I plan to ignore all of these results until somebody I know comes and tells me to check one out: the cost of assessing any of them is too high, and there are too many other papers to read.

comments.author: bmenrigh
comments.content: I think everyone asking for this kind of thing doesn't really understand the scale and complexity of solving a big problem with many agents.For any of the big things I've worked on, it isn't one "prompt", it's a goal that keeps getting updated and a bunch of back-and-forth steering of the model and sub agents, where what the human is saying to guide the model is heavily context dependent on what the model is currently doing or saying. Much of that guidance will ultimately be useless guidance on dead-end explorations. Also, the model will likely have written huge programs to solve things symbolically or simulate things numerically, and both the programs that were written, and the output of those programs are critical to understanding how the model came up with the things that led to a solution.Now, I'd be all for publishing the full transcript, but the transcript is likely to be massive. Gigabytes of text, and reproducing the local computation (often sympy or numpy) may be hundreds or thousands of CPU-hours.

comments.author: bartnp
comments.content: A worthwhile afternoon:- Order a solar panel that allows charging your phone + a usb stick that plugs into both your phone and a computer- Get a small local LLM on your phone- Download a bunch of pdfs of books useful for a lights out scenario, put them on your phone / ereader + your usb stickI recommend information on: homesteading, electronics, methods to obtain food relevant to your location (fishing, farming), handiman stuff, basic health and medicine, local maps and food preservation.Note that on the short term it's probably exposure, violence or disease from bad water/food that kills and it's best to stay home. You're better off cooperating than bunkering in because your odds of surviving harsh periods are much better that way. In most areas it's very difficult to survive entirely self sufficiently on food you grow/forage even if you've practiced for years and have everything already set up. And if you're not that ready, it's hopeless.

comments.author: MandieD
comments.content:
"A man can work from sun to sun,
but a woman's work is never done."The spinning, particularly before spinning wheels became common (and affordable), could be done in parallel to a lot of other tasks - cooking (the waiting portions), walking to town or the fields, watching small children, and once you're used to it, can be done without light.Making yarn from raw wool is my main hobby, and I've fallen into the annual rhythm of sourcing, sorting and scouring (cleaning to remove dirt and excess lanolin) wool in the summer when it's warm enough to suint (ferment the dirty wool in its own sweat, which works way better than it sounds) and then dry the wool outside, carding/combing and spinning in the fall and winter, and finally dyeing the finished yarn mostly in the spring, because I don't want to handle those chemicals indoors... and also so I have something nice to give the people I get the next set of fleeces from, beginning the cycle again.I think we, as a society, have forgotten just how much time went into yarn/thread production before the Industrial Revolution because that was the first major automation target, and most women were happy not to have to do it any more. Plus, being mostly women's work, the details weren't important enough to the people who wrote "serious" books about the economy.

comments.author: alwa
comments.content: One phenomenon I’d not thought of until I encountered it, but that seems obvious in retrospect: in the immediate course of an exogenous shock (like natural disaster or war or large-scale social disruption), people tend to really come through for their neighbors [0].The most reliable pattern seems to be a temporary burst of social cohesion. To the extent that durable negative social outcomes materialize, they tend to (1) roughly follow the contours of the same new material/social circumstances had they developed non-suddenly; and (2) take weeks and maybe months to overcome that initial swell of empathy.In any case I agree that the human side is the important side—we owe a nod to communities like the Amish and religious orders who’ve done a lot of R&D into social cohesion technologies during blue skies![0] (e.g. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7115229/ and https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/028072709801600305 and many others in the genre)

comments.author: postalcoder
comments.content: I don’t think anyone who have yet commented has used the actual model. But, to be fair to the commenters, google has made it very hard for them to do so without spending a ton of money.Neon is a really good model. It’s currently my favorite model to use. Coding-wise, it’s equivalent to Opus 5.5/Fable. Documentation-wise, it is great. If you have access to Neon have it take a crack at simplifying your agents.md. It’s the first model I’ve run that criticized the amount of ceremony in my instructions and suggested solid simplifications. It also makes clean edits to documents without leaving scars of the previous verbiage behind.Art-wise, it’s more capable, in my experience, than Fable. I’ve been using fable/opus heavily to make art assets for my application (I shared in a previous comment that procedural art has completely obviated gpt-image art for me) and I’ve started to run into a wall with how far I could iterate with fable. I had neon take a crack at the assets I struggled to improve and it did a grand job.In terms of working together with a model and how it communicates to you, I love this model. The model knows how to clearly communicate to you. It is such a breath of fresh air over Opus and Fable which, despite the improvements, I feel is actively trying to damage my brain with its unnatural prose. It's hard to describe how it feels to have a model that you feel respects your time and energy with proper writing, and the subsequent delight that arises from the feeling of wanting to engage in smaller details again.Neon has a big model smell, but the miracle and irony is it’s supposedly based on a smaller base model than Carbon. On google’s model page, they previously wrote that Neon shares the same base model as Hydrogen! It is thought that Argon and Carbon share the same base model.My impressions will probably change as I use this for longer than a day, but my initial impression is: I don’t know how google pulled this off.

comments.author: themgt
comments.content: I haven't watched the videos, but Hanson's reasoning here feels like a huge stretch to me:But AI costs to answer a set of fixed but hard questions seems to have fallen roughly ~x10 (in x3-x30) per year over the last four years. And so the number of nations, firms, and orgs who can afford to make, buy, or rent powerful AI is rising fast. This implies that in order to hold constant levels of regulation regarding AIs with particular levels of power, a regulatory regime would have to expand in scope quite fast, and without obvious limit. While at first only specialized AI chips and data-centers might need to be monitored, soon other kinds could also be used to make powerful AIs.We have long seen many regulatory agencies slowly expand their scope, even in contexts of constant public opinion and relevant technology. comments.author: Animats
comments.content:
>  It feels like human society hasn't really even figured out alignment for itself -- i.e. we don't have a good way of making sure that we organize units (businesses, politics, healthcare, etc) in ways that are aligned with 'good outcomes'.Yes. This a fundamental political problem. We don't really know how to organize society for the capabilities we have now, let alone for the ones we get with better AI. Thinking about this too hard results in questioning the underlying assumptions of capitalism. That terrifies many people.Many of the problems with "AI alignment" are the same problems seen with "corporate alignment". We already have AI-assisted corporations. It's tough to separate obnoxious behavior by corporations from obnoxious behavior by AIs. We can easily see this now. Just call customer service for any of the FAANG companies.Piketty's "Capital and Ideology" starts to address this. It's pre-AI, but covers how societies dealt with this historically. Which is not very well. I'm still struggling through that book. Piketty shows that even the French Revolution didn't level out wealth distribution much.  Beheading the aristocrats didn't help.There have been fundamental changes over time. Piketty points out that societies before the industrial revolution were usually tripartite - nobility, priests, and peasants. He's done his homework, and reports that nobility plus priests consistently runs 2% to 4% of the population. Interestingly, there's almost always a priesthood, across a wide range of theologies.But then came manufacturing, and the world changed. The "rise of the middle class" began.
The world became more complicated and interlinked, and a middle class was needed to manage the details.As computers progressed, the middle class was partly replaced by automation. AI is accelerating that, as we can see in new college graduate hiring statistics. Even before AI, about half of US college graduates were in jobs that didn't really need a college degree.
That's getting worse.The default direction of AI in the developed world seems to be a few people at the top, a lot of people at the bottom using their hands, and AIs in the middle. Maybe half the middle class goes.
That's the problem of the next ten years.Robotics isn't good enough yet to replace the operatives at the bottom. That may or may not change. Robots may be too expensive. That's probably the problem of the 2040s.So what do we do now?

comments.author: PaulHoule
comments.content: For a long time I’ve been chewing on this…Back in the 2000’s I was involved with numerous “social” systems before there was Facebook, the thing they all had in common was that we knew we lived or died based on being viral so the most important knob we could turn in the process was the rate at which people completed the onboarding and recommended new people.  So we were obsessive about plugging leaks in our funnel from both a craftsmanship and business standpoint.Today whether it is mobile games or anything else I’m often left wondering if there is anybody left who remembers what it takes to tune up a funnel.  Now I am told that for western mobile games they aren’t even interested in players who would care what the game mechanics are but instead just want to filter for a handful of ‘whales’ who will start spending money when they encounter the slightest speed bump… but still!Right now I trade it back to the time when Facebook discovered its business model,  made virality impossible,  and convinced everybody to pay for traffic.  You’d think the same motivations exist there,  like you can save your money or your investors’ money if you have a good onboarding process so you should but what you find is…. People don’t.I’ve had people blame the OKR/KPI culture for this which has everybody distracted by sub optimization….  But there’s also the problem that the thing you really need to compare customer acquisition cost to is lifetime customer value.  So yeah,  you spend $50 to get a customer to spend $20 where your COGS is $18…. That’s the part you know about and it looks awful and you tell yourself that that LCV will be more than $2 which is true because some of those customers will come back but it’s speculative.  So you think you are practicing ‘quantitative marketing’ but you are like Coca-Cola in the mid 20th century spending on every kind of advertising because you think the brand equity is worth it.

comments.author: Marol
comments.content:
Deranged depiction of wishful thinking. 
These "casinos" as you call them, can be reverse engineered, and bargained to get unbelievable margins. B/E on your ads? Make more creatives. Period. If you are getting sales but you are not profitable yet, it means that you are a few clever decisions away from succeeding. The "just one sale away" is the direct result of skill issues of the founder. The real problem would be getting zero sales or having 0.7 ROAS (which is not bad if you are running subs btw). Your market is crowded? Change the market. Internet advertising gives you one of the best way to iterate in the world. You can test a concept in literal hours instead of days or weeks it would take you to contact right people or even find them. Facebook / google does that for you.Also regarding the last paragraph that says you should step out of the casino. Why is this mutually exclusive? You can use paid ads to get returning customers and have the paid funnels automate your customer acquisition, which gives you even more time to make your existing clients happy. 
Big amount of people that quit paid ads actually forget about the fact, that if you have a client, that was brought to you from paid ads would most likely never be brought to you otherwise. And if he ever comes back to you again, he won't be accounted in the panel. That break even roas might actually be way above profitable, but you just are not accounting all the returning customers that have heard about you from the ads and stayed.It does not mean the ad platforms are perfect though. You can literally get your entire business decimated in a matter of one automated decision that brings your ad account down. And there isn't any real way to secure yourself, other than taking this into account beforehand. Which in turn requires you to become an expert in evasion tactics, which is below optimal when all you wanna do is sell your damn product.Also don't even get me started on Kafkaesque scenarios that you can face when using these platforms.

comments.author: hatthew
comments.content: Sure, we can make some analogy between ads and gambling, and transitively apply that to ad platforms and casinos. But this article frames ad platforms as exploitative entities engineering advertisers to lose money, when the reality is that the ad platforms provide a marketplace, and via the consequences of supply and demand this marketplace can end up being negative ROI for some advertisers.Ads have a positive EV while gambling has a negative EV, which completely changes how the entities hosting these products behave. Casinos try to get you to stay on by tricking you into thinking you have a positive EV, while ad platforms get you to stay on by genuinely trying to give you a positive EV. If you aren't getting positive results on your ads, you genuinely have the agency to adjust your ads to try to get positive EV. Casinos are explicitly engineered to give you negative EV regardless of how you behave, and kick you out if you try to change that (e.g. card counting).If we say that you shouldn't buy the products of an ads platform because the platform tries to get you to buy more, we may as well say you shouldn't buy the products of a grocery store because the store tries to get you to buy more.

If you aren't getting positive results on your ads, you genuinely have the agency to adjust your ads to try to get positive EV. Casinos are explicitly engineered to give you negative EV regardless of how you behave, and kick you out if you try to change that (e.g. card counting).If we say that you shouldn't buy the products of an ads platform because the platform tries to get you to buy more, we may as well say you shouldn't buy the products of a grocery store because the store tries to get you to buy more.

comments.author: PaulHoule
comments.content:
I would like to see this claim justified:   In the Dewey Decimal System, a book on gardening could potentially be in 
   any of the four places in the system that contained gardening content. 
   With Wayfinder, it’s all in the same place.

I think there is always a question of where to file something,  like a book about the history of gardening in England could be filed under gardening or the history of England.  You could do better than old systems but you're not getting it right always.I think the greatest embarrassment in Dewey and Library of Congress (LC) is how they handled computers.  Dewey has a trash section at the beginning and computers wind up right after UFOs and bigfoot but oddly most occult subjects end up in the 130's except for a tiny bit in the 398.4 but my witchy friends would be happy to know The Spiral Dance is filed at 299.LC on the other hand puts almost everything about computers in QA76 except for some clusters in the TK area and some oddly general things in QA75.  (In LC The Spiral Dance is filed along with more lurid books on witchcraft that Dewey files at 133.4)  Instead of "generic" and "math" and in some alternate universe it would have been reasonable to put computers under electronics in 621.3 and in fact you might find a few books there about how gates are constructed in CMOS there if you're lucky.The trouble is that computers expanded to embrace everything so books like "How to process your photographs in Adobe Lightroom" ends up in the 0's that really ought to be filed in the 600's (photography as technology) or the 770s (photography as art.)  Stuff like that ends up in 0's in Dewey but in LC usually gets filed in the TRs,  though if it was like Dewey they'd file photography under the NDs.The advantage a "bookstore-like" system has is that if it isn't set in stone you can change it.

comments.author: jmyeet
comments.content: I'm honestly disappointed at the number of snark comments on HN about PHP. It's like posting 2007 memes. Yes, we all know the story of htmlspecialchars(). We can make fun of "global" when we don't realize "global" actually means "request scoped". We get it.I've always viewed PHP as having these ideal features:1. A stateless functional core. It's cheap to run and quick to start. Compare this to Java or even Python. There's no loading a bunch of class libraries;2. Every request has an environment created then torn down. That means it's hard for a given request handler to leak memory or other resources. You compare this to, say, Java's servlet API (which only really existed because the startup costs were too high) where resource leaking is a real problem and then you get into GC and STW pauses; and3. Every request is single-threaded. This is ideal. Async network/IO requests are handled via extensions. You should never need to spawn a thread in a request handler directly. You eliminate a whole class of bugs by doing this.Is PHP perfect? No. The class separator as the backslash still offends me more than a decade later. I really wish Facebook's Hack had become PHP because it's got a vastly better type system, core collection classes (list, vec, dict) and it did things a decade ago that PHP is only added with this release (eg polling).As for partial functions, the use case seems to be versioning? I actually prefer the Javascript polyfill method here where possible. Don't make users care about this kind of stuff.

comments.author: idoubtit
comments.content:
My main worry with PHP is that its surface constantly grows. This means the language is1. more complex to use (it took years for some parsers to implement the PHP 8.4 property hooks, and I suppose few people can explain how they work with inheritance and traits),
2. more costly to maintain (I remember when the developer of PHP's JIT left, the PHP foundation was worried because no one could understand the JIT code),
3. and has more security risks (critical security releases will continue).I don't disagree with you, but the situation is more nuanced, and PHP's initial promises are now blurred.> 1. A stateless functional core. It's cheap to run and quick to start.Most modern codebases use a framework. And once you have to load Wordpress, Drupal, or even worse, Laravel, then it's no longer cheap and quick.
So PHP added several layers of complexity to mitigate this: an opcode cache, a code-preload system...> 2. Every request has an environment created then torn down.That's no longer always true. When the code preload is enabled, a request can leak into another.> 3. Every request is single-threaded. [...] Async network/IO requests are handled via extensions.You mixing up two different things. The default PHP SAPIs have single-threaded request handlers (though IIRC the default deploy stack of Laravel differs). But the language has a native async feature through Fibers, from which coroutines can be implemented (see amphp/amp).So PHP on the server side is usually like JS on the client side (except for workers): single-threaded with async. Though I haven't seen much use of Fibers in the wild, it's in the language.

comments.author: Jach
comments.content: Yeah, the most shallow "PHP bad" comments are pretty annoying, but they sometimes have a point, and there are always new programmers who don't know any history. One of the bug fixes I saw today was for an issue that's been around for 20 years and is another consequence of PHP's decision (IMO a bad one) to have a unified "stream wrapper" API such that functions named, for example, file_get_contents(), can be passed a URL rather than a file. If that URL was httpS or HTTPS (i.e. an uppercase S), then the bug now fixed was that PHP would ignore TLS and initially connect over port 80 and make the initial request (along with sending whatever else) over plaintext. It could also successfully follow a redirect to actual https but hide that it leaked data in the initial request. This is just such a PHP thing. I've at times acted the apologist for PHP, it was my first language over 20 years ago so I'll always have some fondness for it, but in my heart I do think it fundamentally sucks and can't be evolved to stop sucking.The last time I did any professional work in PHP was probably 2012, though. Since then I've only maintained a couple things I originally made myself, and on rare occasions have written a standalone script or two (I think the last one was about 3 years ago) and it still makes me happy that I can just rsync things up to my site. Thankfully the maintenance work has been very minimal, but in contrast I've not been excited about any PHP changes since the early 5 days, and my upgrades from 5 to 7 to 8 were mostly just going "huh" (though sometimes "Eh? wtf") at the new features while being wary of breaking changes (the upgrade guides over the years have been helpful and there haven't been many breaking changes). comments.author: tristanj
comments.content: It's pretty obvious that Gemini 4 Carbon is not token efficient. It also has relatively low tokens-per-second compared to other models. I can think of several reasons why this is the case:1. Google has huge amounts of cash and compute. Their goal was to train a model that that has the highest quality & frontier performance, not create a model that's efficient to run and serve. They have other models for that, like Hydrogen.2. Google created Carbon without caring for inference costs. DeepMind is subsidized by the rest of Google's empire. Selling inference is an insignificant part of Google's revenue. But for Anthropic and OpenAI, selling inference is their entire business model. Anthropic and OpenAI have enormous incentive to sell as much inference as they can in the most efficient manner. Google doesn't have this incentive.3. They are one of the few companies that can be inefficient. Out of all the frontier labs, Google DeepMind is probably the least constrained by compute. Chinese labs have around 10 to 100 times less compute, so they must release highly optimized models.

comments.author: chriddyp
comments.content: I've tested 75 models so far, and Gemini 4 Carbon is 68th/75 in terms of slowness [1]Looking into it, there are 4 areas that contribute to speed:1. Time-to-first-token is slower than others: 5s (median) to start on a one-line prompt and 11s on a ~130K-token cached prompt, against 2-2.5s for Gemini 4 Hydrogen and 1-5s for GPT, Claude, Grok, Kimi and Qwen. Long tail though: one call took 50 s and one timed out.2. Tokens/s is slower, but not that much: 3-9s for Carbon vs ~5s for Hydrogen.3. It’s not wordy: thinking included, Carbon wrote ~500 output tokens per request vs ~780 for Hydrogen, and less over the whole exam (220K vs 259K). Slow-but-wordy models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Kimi K3.1 Pro write 1,600 to 2,200 per request.4. More thorough, more tool calls: 10.3 model calls per question vs 7.7 for Hydrogen. On data-quality audits it made 17 vs 9, and on our "find the hidden pattern" questions it ran 41 queries on average vs a board median of ~25.The 4th piece is pretty interesting as it’s more about the behavior than the infra. If the task is “find all of the issues”, and the model is very exhaustive in its search, then “time per task” calls it slow but in practice we’d call it thorough.[1] https://plotly.com/blog/gemini-4-carbon-plotly-data-analytic...

posts.abstract: 讨论要点：Cool coincidence. In a past job, I specifically made replacement PCMCIA cards for these (and other) planes. Instead of making cards with a controller and onboard storage, we made cards with an FPGA/mi...

comments.author: jotux
comments.content: Cool coincidence. In a past job, I specifically made replacement PCMCIA cards for these (and other) planes. Instead of making cards with a controller and onboard storage, we made cards with an FPGA/microcontroller and a microSD card soldered to the PCB. We did this specifically because these aircraft use (at least partially) broken implementations of the PCMCIA protocol, and we'd update the bus protocol per aircraft to work around the limitations. None of these planes can just go buy stuff off the street because some large portion just doesn't work because their protocol isn't fully implemented and isn't flexible to deal with variance in timing/speed/etc.A fun story: Our cards had whatever industrial-spec microSD card we could find (16GB, 32GB, etc.), and we'd internally limit the disk size to whatever the platform needed. Almost every aircraft had some specific number of MB they wanted because all of their CONOPS listed it, and they didn't want to update documentation or software to put a different number there. We had a plane that could only use EXACTLY 128MB, but they were currently using 256MB cards and partitioning them to 128MB. We updated the disk size to present as 128MB so they could skip this step, and they specifically told us to put it back to 256MB because they didn't want to update the commissioning process to remove the partitioning step.It was rewarding work, and the card we designed was cheap (~$500 each, which is literally nothing for major platforms like this) and 100% US-designed and made (with the exception of ICs manufactured in the usual places). Still, the procedural and cultural practices of these program offices made it a real struggle to get traction and deploy them widely. Government acquisition is just generally designed around funding primes for current development and then paying through the nose for sustainment later. It was hard to design something for widespread sustainment use because by the time you were done and ready for production, a bunch of parts would be obsolete. Then you'd have to rev the design over and over. We were never allowed to stockpile anything, even if it was trivially cheap, to facilitate production later.

comments.author: spicyjpeg
comments.content: It's worth pointing out that there are actually two main types of PCMCIA memory cards. The most common by far are the ATA cards mentioned here, which are basically CF cards in a different form factor (equivalent to a CF card in a CF-to-PCMCIA adapter) and work by emulating either an IDE hard drive or an ISA IDE controller depending on wiring. While uncommon at this point, CF controller chips are still available and some specialized suppliers do manufacture these cards brand new using modern NAND flash.The much more problematic ones to find a replacement for in 2026 are the so-called "linear" memory-mapped cards, consisting of one or more banks of raw parallel NOR flash with no controller IC. Linear cards were never standardized and the protocol used to interface to parallel flash can vary greatly across chip families, so the vast majority of devices that use them are hardcoded to only accept cards with a specific manufacturer and device ID. Many NOR flash manufacturers from the turn of the century have long discontinued their products and emulating parallel flash using modern FPGAs and microcontrollers is also non-trivial due to their memory-mapped nature, so owners of legacy telecom equipment and original Dance Dance Revolution arcade cabinets [1] are left with pretty much no viable replacement option once the stock cards fail.[1] https://psx-spx.consoledev.net/konamisystem573/#flash-chips-...

comments.author: jotux
comments.content: Another story:PO came to me and asked if our card would work on their plane. We ship them a prototype and it doesn't work. They ship it back and send along a card that does work in the plane. We test it, and the card is just faster. We get the designer of the data box (works at the prime) on the phone and talk to him. Explain that our card works within timing specs but isn't working in the plane reader. He says something along these lines: "Oh, our reader implements the communication specification just fine, but only for fast cards. When we designed the box we wanted to hit a certain read/write speed, so we went out and bought a bunch and found the fastest cards and wrote our VHDL to talk to those cards." After we collected our jaws from the floor we updated our card to run a little faster and it started working. They had a lot of trouble finding commercial cards that worked.And another:One of the hardest parts to find for a PCMCIA card is stamped sheet metal cases. When we made prototypes, we bought case kits where the PCB just dropped in if you followed the PCB outline and used the right 68 pin connector. Around 2020 the companies that made them started to discontinue them, sent out a notice to offer final production batch ordering to do final lifetime buys. I BEGGED a bunch of groups to go order a few thousand, or tens of thousands and just put them in a closet somewhere (they were like $9/each). No one could make the decision in time, they went obsolete. We ended up designing a new machined aluminum case with super tight tolerances and features and it was like 80% of the total $500 cost.

comments.author: bityard
comments.content: You'd be _amazed_ at the red tape and expense required to modernize any part of a military aircraft maintenance system. You have to understand, when the US military orders a new plane, they don't buy only the plane. They buy the blueprints, parts manifest, pilot training curriculum, maintenance manuals, maintenance equipment, etc... literally just about everything except the manufacturing facility where they are built. Each aircraft is its own big program with tens of thousands of people employed by it at any given time. Changing even one small piece of it is a monumental undertaking.Circa 2000, I worked in an avionics shop that serviced (among others) MH-53J helicopter navigation and autopilot systems. The test bench for this system was about 20-feet long end-to-end and was driven by a rack-mount IBM PC with an 8086 running MS-DOS. Storage was a 5MB (or so) pre-IDE hard drive with its own controller. These were... not reliable. And since we were a training base, getting new ones was just about impossible. When the drive died, much of the test bench was useless. I wanted so bad to swap out that drive with some kind of ISA->CompactFlash adapter, but _any_ unauthorized modifications to a test bench or procedure were strictly illegal, even if you knew what you're doing.

The F-16 also uses PCMCIA cards.It's the right size for the job. It's small enough to be easily carried around, and big enough that it can be handled while wearing heavy gloves.

In this application, you want a visible label on the device, since the card contains mission specific data and there are other similar cards around.

comments.author: dlor
comments.content: I also found this independently ahead of disclosure and reported it to Oracle last Friday. My harness found it after a fuzzing run and then turned it into a full RCE chain in the target app I was actually scanning.The harness itself doesn't run with Internet access and I confirmed it didn't access this PR directly, but who knows if this was in the training set itself.Either way, these simultaneous disclosures are incredibly common now. The Ruby issue affecting Gitlab was not only known about for 6 months, it was publicly fixed for 6 months before someone turned it into an RCE. The fix sat on the Ruby dev branch, and it was never pulled into an actual Ruby release until after Gitlab disclosed their own 10.0 vulnerability through it.It's very common for reporters to not realize the impact of a bug, models are very good at turning bugs into RCE chains, and the volume everywhere now means security teams are basically only focused on RCEs.

comments.author: eesmith
comments.content: Having grown up in the US South, I can tell you how -- most houses since the 1960s were designed around A/C, and are incredibly ill-suited if the A/C doesn't work.I know this because I grew up in a house in Florida built in the 1950s, with no A/C. Southern vernacular architecture includes high ceilings (so the heat rises above the people), lots of windows (to let the air go through and heat escape), and with the house raised off the ground (so cooling air flows underneath). While my house didn't have it, another typical design element is a wraparound porch, to provide extra shade and let the windows stay open even when it rains.If you build for A/C in the South then you want a building with good insulation and little airflow, to save on power. If the A/C doesn't run then these places get very warm, humid, and stuffy. Nearly every house is built this way.Further, if you are used to the chill that A/C provides then your body doesn't adjust to the heat.The US Southwest has its own vernacular architecture. The days are hot and the night cool, so use thick adobe walls which take 12 hours for the heat of day to seep through. Close the windows in the morning to keep the cool in, open them at night to cool off, while the heat from the walls keeps the inside more moderate.

You see, at least when we're talking about summer heat AC, you can just build more of the panels and feed the much flatter baseload to industry that prefers to run the capital intensive machinery not only when the sun shines high during the summer.If we're talking about winter heating in for example German climates, you'd have to over build so much solar capacity to handle cold winters (even if we're willing to turn on fuel burning supplementary heaters for a statistically single digit number of days per year) that you have severe excess in summer.You'd turn most factories (those with decently high electricity draw per capital expenditure) off for about a month worth of days in winter, usually combining this with scheduled maintenance, and:To further shift large amounts of country-scale power consumption from year-round/winter to only sunny summer days:
try to set up electrical refining of (purified) iron ore into (metallic) iron at larger solar farms where you could recycle their grid connection and their AC/DC converters together with already normalized (for there) local batteries (to shift delivery of half the production from around noon to the night, which reduces the AC/DC converter capacity and the AC grid connection/transformer size requirements).
There are realistic low-temperature electrolysis options for electro-chemically splitting the oxygen off of the iron (purified iron ore is iron oxide) like Siderwin [0] and even near-room-temperature options like Electra [1].For scale, [0] claims replacing the production of the existing coal-based iron ore refining plants of Europe with Siderwin would require 471 TWh/year in additional electricity in the grid; [2] claims the EU (without the overall insignificant island Malta, as it's not connected to the continental grid in a way that'd be readily suited to inclusion in these common-measurement-definitions statistics) produced 2497.3 TWh in the entire year of 2024, of which 237.6 TWh were solar.Thus, it's overall "not that much" extra production capacity that'd even be spent on this (assuming an essentially-fully renewable grid, let's call it 99% by yearly aggregate electricity production):

Hence the proposal/suggestion to move it to the DC side of solar farms that are large enough to warrant the staffing/infrastructure overhead.[0]: https://industrydecarbonization.com/news/making-steel-with-e...

comments.content: Thankfully it's not a zero sum game. We aren't up against serious limits on how much solar power can be built.If producing solar panels is profitable, then your purchase gives the manufacturer capital it can use to expand production. comments.author: tombert
comments.content: My favorite uncle died from pancreatic cancer when I was a teenager. I remember at the time I quickly looked up the survivability rates of pancreatic cancer and was immediately sad to see it was nearly zero [1].For the next few months, there was a roller coaster of hearing about his new treatments, sometimes seeming effective where we would convince ourselves that he's going to get better, only for him to take a turn for the worse.  This kept happening until, of course, he died.  I was sad he was dead but the combination of the cancer and the chemo seemed really miserable so I was at least happy he wasn't in pain anymore.This happened around the time Patrick Swayze died from pancreatic cancer, and a bit before Steve Jobs, and it was at least a little reassuring that this disease didn't spare even obscenely wealthy people.   I hope we figure out better treatments for it, and this seems promising.[1] At least when caught late, which it often is and was for him.

comments.author: thinkcontext
comments.content: So many impacted by cancer in this thread, I've also been in the position where you feel powerless when someone close to you is diagnosed.  I try to take opportunities like this to remind people that there are some types of cancer (and other conditions) that you can help other people with through a bone marrow transplant.Cancers like leukemia, melanoma, lymphoma and conditions like aplastic anemia, immune, autoimmune disorders can be treated by infusing the patient with compatible bone marrow stem cells from a donor.  Finding a compatible donor can be difficult, on average in the general population its on the order of 1:10,000 to find a match.  For that reason there's a registry that people can submit a cheek swab to.  In my case I joined the registry about 15 years ago when someone in my extended friend circle had leukemia.  A swab drive was organized to find her a donor, which eventually happened and she wound up beating it.  I didn't match her but a few years ago I matched another patient and wound up donating.In the US the registry is National Marrow Donor Program.  Signup on their website and they will send you a free swab kit.https://www.nmdp.org/

comments.author: tptacek
comments.content: There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.

comments.author: ggm
comments.content: Done properly, for a signature to work you need different in-page offsets from the binding point for the left and right faces of "outside" and the innermost "inside and outside" sheets: the thickness of the paper affects the folding and so affects the offset of the page edge from the actual paper edge after guillotineing.I fell down this rabbit hole about 3 decades ago playing with the various postscript n-up tools, and looking at the outcome. I was working with an A3 printer and hitting alignment problems on 16 page signatures. I do not think I worked out how to fix it, other than heuristical sub-adjustments.After 8 pages, the bend radius difference is probably 1-2mm so it's definitely visible.

comments.author: meowvia
comments.content: A fixed words-per-page number is hard because it swings a lot with type size, leading, margins, and how many headings or images break up the text. At 10pt with normal margins, each A6-ish page in this layout holds roughly 180-220 words of plain prose, but that's a rough guide, not a layout rule.For the markdown editor idea, I'd find a per-section word count more useful than a single estimate: split the draft at headings, show the running count against the page it will land on, and flag sections that overflow.
